canonical_statement: The study aimed to identify risk factors for bacterial infection after firearm injury and evaluate the association between bacterial infection and mortality among US adults hospitalized with firearm injuries.
The cohort used Premier Healthcare Database records from January 2019 through May 2021 and included hospitals contributing microbiologic data.
The cohort included 24,024 patients from 323 US hospitals; mean age was 32.9 years and 85.3% were male.

population.label: US adults hospitalized with firearm injury at 323 hospitals contributing microbiologic data to the Premier Healthcare Database

canonical_statement: Bacterial infection required a positive culture from any source plus antibiotics started within 2 days and continued for at least 4 days or until discharge; cultures positive for fungal pathogens or elements were excluded.

outcome.definition: Positive culture plus qualifying antibiotic treatment

canonical_statement: Early infection was defined as infection during the index hospitalization, whereas late infection was defined as infection developing during 90-day follow-up.
Multivariable logistic regression evaluated clinical factors associated with infection among patients who survived at least 1 day, with separate models for early and late infection.
The regression models included demographics, insurance type, firearm type, injury intent and severity, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, and surgery involving different body regions.
Median antibiotic duration in the overall firearm-injury cohort was 1 day, with an IQR of 0 to 1 day.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that bacterial infection was relatively common during the initial hospitalization, new infection during follow-up was rare, and bacterial infection was not independently associated with mortality among patients surviving at least 1 night.
The study relied on administrative data and diagnosis codes.
The infection definition was deliberately specific and required positive cultures plus antibiotic treatment, which may not capture empirically treated infections without qualifying culture evidence.
Surgical procedure type and New Injury Severity Score were used as proxies for acute illness severity.
Complete follow-up data may not have been available for all patients.
The authors reported no conflicts of interest.
The article directs readers to supplemental content for the data sharing statement.
